tagline.text: Philippine military history and tanks inside the Army headquarters at Fort Bonifacio

location.label: Location
location.text: Philippine Army headquarters compound (Lawton Avenue), Fort Bonifacio, Taguig City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~600 (including transport; confirm the admission fee locally)

children.text: A military museum inside Fort Bonifacio in Taguig, home of the Philippine Army headquarters. Founded in 1979 as the Army's history gallery, it shows uniforms, weapons and colors indoors and tanks and artillery outdoors. Because it sits inside a military compound, advance booking is required.

The Philippine Army Museum is a military history museum run by the Philippine Army itself, located inside Fort Bonifacio in Taguig City, Metro Manila. It is not far from the skyscrapers of Bonifacio Global City (BGC), but the museum stands inside the Army headquarters compound rather than on an ordinary street, so the atmosphere is completely different. Once you pass the guardhouse and enter the large base, you will find an outdoor display of old tanks and cannons set among neat lawns and military buildings.
The museum is said to date from

. In the late 1980s, the Army commander at the time, General Mariano Adalem, had the former US Army commanding general's headquarters converted into a museum and library, and the neighboring Fort Bonifacio Tunnel was also incorporated into the exhibits; both are said to have opened together in

. In the 1990s, much of Fort Bonifacio was turned into today's BGC business and residential district, and the museum moved to its present spot in the Army compound. As a result, older guides sometimes give an address around MacArthur Drive, so be sure to confirm the current location before you go.

Fort Bonifacio began around 1901, during the American colonial period, as a US military base called Fort William McKinley (a land title dated 1902 is also cited). On May 14, 1949, it was handed over to the Philippine government. It became the permanent Philippine Army headquarters in 1957 and was later renamed after the revolutionary Andrés Bonifacio, though sources differ on when the renaming happened. Today it is home to the Philippine Army headquarters. As you tour the museum, the story overlaps with the history of this land, from US base to Japanese occupation to Philippine Army headquarters.

This is not a glamorous tourist attraction. Instead, it lets you see in one place what equipment and uniforms the Philippine military used and what battles it fought, which makes it a surprisingly rewarding half-day for travelers interested in military history or families who want to show children real tanks. Because it is a visit to a military base, you cannot simply turn up as you would at an ordinary museum; contacting them in advance to get permission is the rule. The tunnel story is also worth knowing. According to Wikipedia and similar sources, the Fort Bonifacio Tunnel was used from the late 1930s (some sources say 1910) to move military supplies, and in
October 1941

digging began for an underground air warning facility. After Japanese forces took the base in 1942, they extended the tunnel and used it as a shelter for senior officers, and they are said to have left the base in
February 1945
. Sources give different construction dates, so the exact chronology is hard to pin down.

blocks.title: Outdoor tank and armored vehicle yard

children.text: In front of the museum, retired tanks, armored vehicles and cannons stand in rows. The M41 Walker Bulldog light tank, FV101 Scorpion, Cadillac Gage Commando and M113 armored personnel carrier are among those listed. You can see their size and gun barrels up close, which also makes for good photos.

Weapons such as the OTO Melara Mod 56 howitzer, M3 105mm light howitzer, M40 105mm recoilless rifle and Type 96 25mm anti-aircraft/anti-tank gun are displayed outdoors. Equipment from different countries sits side by side, giving you a sense of the Philippine Army's armament history.

The indoor gallery holds explanatory panels on the Army's founding and development, along with military colors and unit flags. It is air-conditioned, so you can read at a relaxed pace even on hot days. Exhibits are sometimes rearranged, so follow the on-site guidance.

Uniforms from different eras, medals, helmets, packs and other personal equipment are on display. It is fun to compare how clothing changed over time. Exhibits are sometimes rearranged, so follow the on-site guidance.

Firearms such as rifles and pistols, and dioramas recreating battle scenes, let you picture combat situations that words alone cannot convey. It is reported that, as of 2018, there was also an exhibit on the Battle of Marawi.

blocks.title: The story of the Fort Bonifacio Tunnel

children.text: The museum has long been presented together with the history of the Fort Bonifacio Tunnel. The tunnel is said to be about

long and was used in both the US and Japanese periods (some sources say only about 730 m remains today). However, the tunnel itself is reported to have been closed to the public since around 1995, so do not expect to go inside.
The museum is also listed under the name Philippine Army Museum Library and Archives. Reading access for research purposes may require a separate procedure, so ask before you visit.
Visitor reviews mention a small souvenir shop. Whether it is open and what it sells vary, so check locally.
Save your booking confirmation on your phone, bring your ID (passport) and set out from BGC. Follow the entry time and gate you were given when you booked.
Complete the visit procedure at the Army compound guardhouse and head to the museum. The base is large, so confirm your transport in advance.
Start with the outdoor yard and look around the tanks and cannons. The sun gets strong by midday, so it is easier to see the outdoor area in the morning.
Go into the indoor gallery and see the Army history panels, uniforms, firearms and dioramas in turn. Ask staff where photography is allowed.
Wrap up the indoor visit and, if a guide is available, ask any questions you have. Visit the souvenir shop only if it is open.
Return to BGC for lunch, then continue to a nearby park, a shopping mall or the Manila American Cemetery.
Many sources say the museum closes around 4 PM, so it is safest to start in the morning.

From central Manila (Malate, Ermita, Intramuros) or Makati, the simplest way is a Grab or taxi straight to the entrance of the Army headquarters at Fort Bonifacio. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so leave a margin.
From the airport (MNL), take a Grab or taxi toward BGC and then enter the Army compound. During rush hours, EDSA and the C-5 area are very congested.
Ride-hailing cars may reach the compound entrance but not go inside, so ask how to get around inside when you book.
It is safest to enter both the museum name and "Fort Bonifacio Army headquarters" as the destination.
One travel guide says to enter through Gate 6 and take a P2 jeepney, getting off near the museum. Gates and routes can change, so follow the method you were given when you booked.
The base is large and some stretches are far to walk. Do not overdo it in the midday heat.
The museum is mostly indoors, but the outdoor area with the tanks and cannons is a big part of the visit, so the weather matters. The dry season is more comfortable.

Weekday mornings are best. Many sources list opening days as Monday to Friday, and some say weekend visits are possible only for group tours or special requests, so ask in advance if you want to go on a weekend.

The area around the museum is a military facility with no lodging, but nearby BGC has many hotels, serviced apartments and malls. If your trip is built around the museum, staying in BGC is the most convenient.

It is safest to assume you cannot get a meal at the museum. Before or after your visit, use the restaurants and cafes around BGC High Street or Market! Market!. There are many Korean and Japanese restaurants as well, which makes choosing easy for Korean travelers.

Once you are back in BGC, there are plenty of convenience stores and pharmacies, so it is a good place to buy water, snacks and sunscreen before your visit. The museum area is a place for viewing, so do not expect many amenities. Plan lunch for after 12 noon, and see the museum first in the morning.

The most important preparation is booking ahead. One travel guide says foreign tourists should contact the museum by email or phone about three weeks (21 days) in advance, and locals at least one week ahead. Korean travelers should leave plenty of time, following the foreigner timeline.
When you book, you may be asked for your visit date, number of people, nationality and passport details, so have them ready.
Local guides say it is open from around 9 AM to around 4 PM on weekdays, but hours differ by source. Be sure to confirm the opening hours when you book.
Bring your passport (or ID) on the day. Entry to a military base involves identity checks.
Photography is generally allowed outdoors, but some indoor exhibits may be restricted. Do not use flash, and ask staff first before filming video.
Neat clothing is better than shorts and flip-flops. Keep in mind that this is a military facility.
Do not photograph military facilities, soldiers or guarded areas. Follow staff instructions on what is allowed.
A visit usually takes 1–2 hours, and longer with a guide.
The compound is large, so save the museum's location in your map app and ask the entrance guard once more for directions. Map pins for military sites are sometimes inaccurate.

If you are interested in history, read a short summary of Fort Bonifacio and the tunnel before you go and the exhibits will feel far more three-dimensional. Looking up the names of a few tanks online is also a good idea.
Because the museum is inside a military base, you may be refused entry if you turn up without a booking. Check the latest announcements.
Opening hours, days, admission and booking rules differ by source and change often. Confirm directly with the museum or the Army just before your visit.
The Fort Bonifacio Tunnel has been closed to the public since around 1995, and plans for restoration are reported. Do not go expecting to enter it.
Inside the base, follow the instructions of soldiers and guards, and do not enter areas that are not designated.
Ride-hailing drivers sometimes do not know the locations inside the base. Take a screenshot of the destination name and entrance.
It is very hot at midday. Bring water and a hat for the outdoor exhibit area.
A World War II American war cemetery located in the same Fort Bonifacio area. It is a short ride away and pairs well with a military history day.
A new city district close to the museum, with restaurants, cafes and malls that suit lunch and a rest.
A financial and shopping district that connects easily to a city itinerary.
On another day, head toward Intramuros and build a museum route together with the National Museum.
